summary: Qualitative geometric optics for 11–12 year-olds: the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal), plane-mirror virtual images (upright, same size, laterally inverted, equal distance behind), and refraction as a speed-change at a boundary that bends an angled ray toward the normal on entering an optically denser (slower) medium and away on leaving it. Core activities let learners vary an incoming ray and observe how the outgoing ray responds, so the law and the speed-change cause are discovered rather than recited. Snell's law and refractive index are deliberately deferred. Supporting activities cover reference diagrams, checks of the exit-case and normal-measuring pitfalls, and hands-on phenomena (bent pencil, apparent depth).
misconceptions: Measuring angles from the mirror/surface instead of from the normal — the single most frequent geometric error.
Overgeneralising 'denser medium → bends toward the normal' and forgetting the ray bends AWAY from the normal when it exits into the rarer medium.
Confusing reflection with refraction, or thinking a ray does only one at a boundary (light can partially reflect AND refract at the same surface).
Believing light travels in a curve as it bends, rather than travelling straight in each medium and changing direction abruptly at the boundary.
Thinking the OBJECT (e.g. the pencil) physically bends, rather than the light rays from it bending so the eye is deceived.
Teleological 'the light chooses the fastest/shortest path' reasoning offered as a mechanism instead of the speed-change cause.
Assuming the virtual image in a plane mirror is BEHIND the glass 'on' the mirror, or that it is real light, rather than a construction where rays only appear to come from behind.
Assuming a ray entering along the normal (0°) still bends — it changes speed but not direction.

activities.title: Ray bench: discover the reflection law and the refraction bend
steps: Aim one light ray at a flat mirror and vary the angle of the incoming ray; for several angles, measure both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection FROM the normal (the dashed perpendicular at the point the ray meets the surface), and record the pairs.
State the pattern you find between the two angles in your own words before being told any rule.

Place an object in front of the mirror, trace at least two rays from the same point on it to the mirror and back, then extend the reflected rays backward (as dashed lines) behind the mirror to locate where they appear to meet; mark this virtual image and check that it is upright, the same size as the object, and the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front — and note that it is laterally inverted (left and right swapped).

Swap the mirror for a rectangular (parallel-sided) glass block or water tank. Send the ray in at an angle and describe which way it bends on entering (toward or away from the normal) and which way it bends on leaving the far side.
Set the ray to travel exactly along the normal (0° incidence) and observe whether it changes direction; then tilt it by a small amount and observe again.
If the activity provides a speed indicator, note how the ray's speed changes inside the denser medium and relate that change to whether and which way the ray bends.

If a medium control is available (air → water → glass), switch to an optically denser medium (one where light travels more slowly) and, keeping the same angle of incidence, describe what happens to the size of the bend.
activities.insight: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection when both are measured from the normal; and a ray bends because it changes speed at a boundary — slowing (air→glass/water) bends it toward the normal, speeding up (glass/water→air) bends it away, while a ray along the normal changes speed but not direction.

activities.title: Why a mirror images but paper does not: specular vs diffuse
steps: Shine a bundle of parallel rays at a smooth surface (mirror) and at a rough surface (paper); observe and sketch what happens to the rays in each case.
Note that on the smooth surface the parallel rays stay parallel after reflecting, while on the rough surface they scatter in many directions.
Check that each individual ray still obeys angle in = angle out from the local normal, even on the rough surface — the difference is that the rough surface tilts the normal differently at each point.
Sort a set of surfaces (polished metal, still water, paper, matte wall, etc.) into those that form a clear image and those that do not, and explain your sorting using the parallel-vs-scatter idea.
activities.insight: A mirror forms a clear image because its smooth surface keeps reflected rays parallel (specular reflection); a rough surface scatters rays (diffuse reflection) so no image forms — but both obey the law of reflection locally, so the difference is surface smoothness, not a different law.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: the reappearing coin and the bent pencil
steps: Place a coin at the bottom of an opaque mug, then move your head until the coin is just hidden behind the rim, and keep your head still from then on.
Predict what will happen to your view of the coin as a friend slowly pours water into the mug, and write down WHY before anything is poured.
Pour the water (keeping your head still) and record what you actually saw.
Draw the path of a light ray from the coin, through the water surface, to your eye — showing where it bends and which way — to explain the illusion.
Repeat the reasoning for a pencil standing in a glass of water that looks bent or broken at the surface: explain that it is the light rays that bend, not the pencil.
Discuss the probe questions: would a straight-on (0°) ray change direction? Is there really light behind a mirror where the image appears? Would a much denser material bend the ray more?
activities.insight: Refraction at the water surface bends light from the coin/pencil so it appears to come from a different place; the object itself does not move or bend — the eye is deceived by the bent rays, and tracing the ray path explains everyday illusions like apparent depth.

activities.title: Two-tier diagnostic: both boundaries of one ray
steps: Consider a ray of light that goes from air INTO a glass block, travels through it, and comes back OUT into the air on the far side.
Describe how the ray bends at EACH boundary — going in and coming out — and state whether it bends toward or away from the normal in each case.
Explain WHY it bends at each boundary in terms of the speed change.
Answer a direction question: a ray goes from glass into air — which way does it bend? (Watch the tempting but wrong 'toward the normal' answer.)
Trace the full path of the ray through a rectangular (parallel-sided) air→glass→air block, including the exit bend, and show that the emerging ray is parallel to the incident ray.
activities.insight: Which way a ray bends depends on whether it speeds up or slows down at that particular boundary — so a single angled ray bends toward the normal entering the glass and away on leaving, emerging parallel to the incident ray for a parallel-sided block; this cannot be answered by one memorised rule applied to both boundaries.

activities.title: Labelled ray diagram as a reference and vocabulary primer
steps: Study a labelled ray diagram showing a ray reflecting off a mirror and refracting through a block, with the normal, angle of incidence, angle of reflection, angle of refraction, virtual image, and specular/diffuse insets marked.
Reveal and read each callout: the normal is the perpendicular from which every angle is measured; the emergent ray is bent away from the normal because it speeds up leaving the glass.
Use the diagram to name parts and recall vocabulary before or alongside the hands-on ray-bench work.
activities.insight: A clear reference diagram fixes the vocabulary — normal, incidence, reflection, refraction, virtual image, specular/diffuse — and shows the canonical ray paths, supporting the active investigations.

checkQuestion: A ray of light goes from air INTO a glass block, travels through it, and comes back OUT into the air on the other side. Describe how the ray bends at EACH boundary — going in, and coming out — and explain why it bends.
checkAnswer: Entering the glass (air to glass, a denser, slower medium) the ray bends TOWARD the normal; leaving the glass (glass to air, faster) it bends AWAY from the normal, so it emerges parallel to the way it came in. The bending happens because the light changes speed as it crosses each boundary.
